questions.question: What is the definition of $P(A\mid B)$ when $P(B)>0$?
questions.explanation: Conditioning on $B$ restricts attention to outcomes in $B$, so we measure how much of $B$ also lies in $A$: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$, valid when $P(B)>0$.
questions.source_support: The definition gives $P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $P(A)P(B)$ is the joint probability only when $A,B$ are independent; it is not the definition of conditioning.
$P(A\cup B)$ puts a union in the numerator, but conditioning asks how much of $B$ lies in $A$ — that is the intersection $A\cap B$, not the union.
$\dfrac{P(B)}{P(A)}$ is not the conditional-probability formula: $P(B\mid A)$ would require $P(A\cap B)$ in the numerator, while $P(A\mid B)$ divides the intersection by $P(B)$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: What condition is needed to define $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: The definition divides by $P(B)$, so it only makes sense when $P(B)>0$; otherwise the denominator is zero and $P(A\mid B)$ is undefined.
questions.source_support: The definition assumes $P(B)>0$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $P(A)=0$ is a condition on $A$, but the division is by $P(B)$, so it is $P(B)$ that must be positive, not $P(A)$.
Disjointness is not required: if $A,B$ are disjoint with $P(B)>0$, then $P(A\mid B)=0$ is still perfectly defined.
$A=B^c$ is a special structural relationship, not a condition for the definition to exist.

questions.question: How should conditional probability be interpreted?
options: As chance before any information is known
As the number of outcomes in the sample space
As the complement of ordinary probability
As chance after learning that the condition has occurred
questions.explanation: $P(A\mid B)$ updates the probability of $A$ once you know $B$ has happened — it is the chance of $A$ measured within the outcomes where $B$ occurred.
questions.source_support: The interpretation says conditional probability measures chance after learning that a condition has occurred.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: 'Chance before any information' is the prior $P(A)$, i.e. the unconditional probability; conditioning is precisely what happens AFTER the information arrives.
This describes a count of outcomes, not a probability at all.
Conditioning is not complementation: $P(A\mid B)$ is not $1-P(A)$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: If events $B_1,B_2$ partition $S$ (both with positive probability), then $P(A)=$
questions.explanation: This is the law of total probability: split $A$ across the partition and weight each conditional by how likely its block is, $P(A)=P(A\mid B_1)P(B_1)+P(A\mid B_2)P(B_2)$.
questions.source_support: The multiplication rule gives $P(A\cap B_i)=P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i)$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: This pairs each conditional with the OTHER block's probability; total probability multiplies $P(A\mid B_i)$ by its OWN weight $P(B_i)$.
$P(A)P(B_1)P(B_2)$ is a product of marginals (an independence-style expression) and has nothing to do with reconstructing $P(A)$ from a partition.
$P(B_1\mid A)+P(B_2\mid A)$ conditions the wrong way and in fact sums to $1$, not to $P(A)$.

questions.question: Viewed as a function of $A$, is $P(\cdot\mid B)$ itself a probability (with $P(S\mid B)=1$)?
options: Yes; it obeys all probability axioms ($P(S\mid B)=1$)
No; conditioning can push it above $1$
No; some conditional values come out negative
questions.explanation: Fixing $B$, the map $A\mapsto P(A\mid B)$ is non-negative, gives $P(S\mid B)=P(B)/P(B)=1$, and is additive over disjoint $A$ — so it satisfies the probability axioms.
questions.source_support: $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: It cannot exceed $1$: since $A\cap B\subseteq B$, the numerator $P(A\cap B)\le P(B)$, so the ratio is at most $1$.
It cannot be negative: $P(A\cap B)\ge 0$ and $P(B)>0$, so the ratio is $\ge 0$.
It is a probability for every event $A$, not only when $A=B$; $A=B$ just gives the particular value $1$.

questions.question: If $P(A\cap B)=0.2$ and $P(B)=0.5$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: Apply the definition directly: $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{0.2}{0.5}=0.4$.
questions.source_support: The definition is $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.

option_explanations: $0.7=0.2+0.5$ adds the two probabilities, but the definition divides.
$0.1=0.2\times0.5$ multiplies them, which is the joint-probability direction, not the conditional.
$2.5=0.5/0.2$ inverts the ratio, giving a value above $1$ that cannot be a probability.

questions.question: A die roll is known to be even. What is the probability it is six?
questions.explanation: Knowing the roll is even shrinks the sample space to $\{2,4,6\}$; exactly one of these is six, so the probability is $1/3$.
questions.source_support: The examples mention the chance that a die roll is six given that it is even.

$1/2$ is $P(\text{even})$ itself ($3/6$), not the chance of six among the evens.
$2/3$ is the chance of NOT rolling six among $\{2,4,6\}$.

questions.question: If $A\subseteq B$ and $P(B)>0$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: If $A\subseteq B$ then $A\cap B=A$, so $P(A\mid B)=\dfrac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}=\dfrac{P(A)}{P(B)}$.
questions.source_support: Conditional probability uses $P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $P(B)/P(A)$ inverts the ratio; with $A\subseteq B$ the definition gives $P(A)/P(B)$, which is $\le 1$.
$P(A)+P(B)$ adds the probabilities, which has no basis in the definition.
$1-P(B)$ is a complement unrelated to conditioning on $B$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ are disjoint and $P(B)>0$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: Disjoint means $A\cap B=\varnothing$, so $P(A\cap B)=0$ and $P(A\mid B)=0/P(B)=0$: knowing $B$ happened rules $A$ out.
questions.source_support: The definition uses the intersection probability in the numerator.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: $P(A)$ would equal $P(A\mid B)$ only under independence. Here disjointness gives $P(A\cap B)=0$, so conditioning on $B$ makes $A$ impossible and the conditional probability is $0$.
$1$ would mean $A$ is certain given $B$, the opposite of disjoint.
$P(B)$ is unrelated; the numerator $P(A\cap B)$ is $0$, so the answer is $0$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).

questions.question: How does the multiplication rule follow from conditional probability?
options: Replace every conditional probability by a complement
Rearrange $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$ to get $P(A\cap B)=P(B)P(A\mid B)$
questions.explanation: Multiplying both sides of $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$ by $P(B)$ gives the multiplication rule $P(A\cap B)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B)$.
questions.source_support: The key results state that the multiplication rule follows from the definition.
questions.polish_notes: Quality round 9: rebalanced correct-answer positions to remove option-index guessing cue
option_explanations: Complements are not part of the derivation; you simply clear the denominator.
The multiplication rule holds in general and does not assume disjointness (disjointness would force $P(A\cap B)=0$).
Adding $P(A)+P(B)$ belongs to unions/inclusion–exclusion, not to the product $P(A\cap B)$.

questions.question: Why can $P(A\mid B)$ differ from $P(A)$?
options: Learning that $B$ occurred can change the relevant reference cases
Conditional probabilities are always larger than ordinary probabilities
questions.explanation: Conditioning on $B$ changes which outcomes count as possible (only those in $B$), so the fraction of them that lie in $A$ can differ from $A$'s share of the whole space.
questions.source_support: The interpretation says conditioning changes the reference situation to cases where the condition is true.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: Conditioning can make a probability larger OR smaller than $P(A)$ — it is not always larger.
$P(A\mid B)$ depends heavily on $A$ through the numerator $P(A\cap B)$; it does not ignore $A$.
Conditioning restricts the sample space to $B$, it does not remove every outcome (that would leave nothing to measure).

questions.question: Bayes' rule expresses $P(B\mid A)$ using which quantities?
options: $P(A\cap B)$ alone, with no other terms
questions.explanation: Bayes' rule reverses the conditioning: $P(B\mid A)=\dfrac{P(A\mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}$, so it needs $P(A\mid B)$, the prior $P(B)$, and the normaliser $P(A)$.
questions.source_support: Conditional probability is $P(A\mid B)=P(A\cap B)/P(B)$.
questions.rewrite_notes: Hand-authored explanation + per-option explanations (why each wrong option is wrong + the likely misread).
option_explanations: $P(A)$ alone cannot recover a reversed conditional; you also need the forward conditional and the prior.
$P(B\mid A)$ is the very quantity you are computing — you cannot define it in terms of itself.
$P(A\cap B)$ alone is not enough: turning it into $P(B\mid A)$ still requires dividing by $P(A)$.

questions.question: If $P(B)=0.25$ and $P(A\mid B)=0.6$, what is $P(A\cap B)$?
questions.explanation: By the multiplication rule, $P(A\cap B)=P(B)\,P(A\mid B)=0.25\times0.6=0.15$.
questions.source_support: The multiplication rule follows from conditional probability.

questions.question: If $A$ and $B$ are independent and $P(B)>0$, what is $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: Independence means knowing $B$ tells you nothing about $A$, so $P(A\mid B)=P(A)$ (equivalently $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$).
questions.source_support: Independence: $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$.

option_explanations: $0$ is what disjointness gives when $P(B)>0$, because then $A\cap B=\varnothing$. Independence instead leaves the probability of $A$ unchanged.
$1$ would mean $B$ guarantees $A$, a strong dependence, not independence.
$P(B)$ is the wrong quantity; independence returns $P(A)$, the probability of the event being conditioned.

questions.question: In a group of $30$ students, $12$ study statistics and $6$ study both statistics and economics. What is the probability of economics given statistics?
questions.explanation: Condition on studying statistics, so the denominator is the $12$ statistics students; of these $6$ also study economics, giving $6/12$.
questions.source_support: Conditioning changes the reference situation to the cases where the condition is true.
option_explanations: $6/30$ divides the overlap by EVERYONE — that is the unconditional $P(\text{both})$, not the conditional.
$12/30$ is $P(\text{statistics})$, the probability of the conditioning event, not of economics given statistics.
$12/6=2$ inverts the ratio and exceeds $1$, so it cannot be a probability.

questions.question: Why is $P(A\mid B)$ not generally the same as $P(B\mid A)$?
options: The denominators $P(B)$ and $P(A)$ are generally different
The two expressions always use the same denominator
Conditional probability is symmetric by definition

option_explanations: They do NOT use the same denominator: one divides by $P(B)$, the other by $P(A)$.
Conditional probability is directional, not symmetric — that asymmetry is exactly the point.
The intersection does not change order ($A\cap B=B\cap A$), so the numerators are identical; the difference is in the denominator.
